newsitem.title: USA: Fed says bank consumer loan standards tightening.
newsitem.headline: Fed says bank consumer loan standards tightening.

text.p: Banks continued tightening their requirements for consumers seeking to borrow money over the past three months, according to a survey of senior loan officers issued on Tuesday by the Federal reserve.

"Just under half of the banks tightened their standards for approving credit card applications, and a quarter tightened standards for other consumer loans, similar to those found on the August survey," the Fed said.
The survey was based on interviews with loan officers at more than 80 large U.S. banks and branches of foreign banks operating in the United States.

The Fed survey found that banks apparently were more willing to lend to companies than to individuals. It said there was "continued easing of credit supply for businesses, but some pullback for households."

Many banks said they had eased their terms for lending to companies. "However, a large number of banks raised standards for credit-card lending and many tightened standards for other consumer lending," the Fed reported.
The last such survey was issued on Aug 23.
Demand for loans was less vigorous in November than it was in August.

Commercial and industrial loan demand was steady, though more people sought commercial real estate loans. "Several banks reported weaker demand from households, including demand for mortgages and for consumer loans," the Fed said.
The latest survey asked a series of questions about banks' use of credit-scoring models for selecting people to solicit credit cards and in some cases to set terms on accounts.
The models are generally designed to predict defaults or delinquencies and sometimes to predict bankruptcies.
"Nearly two thirds of the respondents indicated that their models had been too optimistic over the past year, predicting better outcomes than actually occurred," the survey found.
